blogs.title: Who Can Enforce Penalties? The Eighth Circuit Limits Private Actions Under Minnesota's Payment of Wages Act
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Eighth Circuit's statutory interpretation of Minnesota's Payment of Wages Act (MPWA), focusing on the court's holding that only the Commissioner of Labor may seek average daily wage penalties under § 181.101. The post examines the court's use of the 'legislature knows how' canon—comparing § 181.101 to §§ 181.13 and 181.14, which expressly authorize employees to seek penalties—and discusses the broader implications for private enforcement of wage-and-hour laws in Minnesota. It also considers how this interpretive approach reflects a broader judicial trend of strictly construing statutory penalty provisions against private rights of action.

blogs.title: Standing to Seek Penalties Payable to the State: Laidlaw's Reach After Full Compensation
blogs.description: This post examines the Eighth Circuit's mootness and standing analysis regarding Cohen's MFLSA statutory penalty claim, which arose after Consilio fully compensated Cohen for overtime wages and liquidated damages. The post explores the tension between Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw—which held that civil penalties payable to the government can provide redress to citizen plaintiffs—and the mootness doctrine's requirement of a continuing personal injury. It also analyzes Judge Kobes's special concurrence, which questions whether Laidlaw's logic extends to MFLSA penalties given the differences between the statutory schemes, and considers the broader doctrinal uncertainty about when plaintiffs retain Article III standing to pursue penalties that flow to the state rather than to themselves.

blogs.title: The Waiver Trap: Procedural Missteps in Employment Class Action Appeals
blogs.description: This post examines the procedural pitfalls that doomed Cohen's MWTA notice claim and his request for injunctive relief. The court affirmed the dismissal of the MWTA claim due to Cohen's failure to cite statutory authority for civil penalties or develop meaningful argument, and declined to consider his revised injunctive relief request because it was raised for the first time in summary judgment briefing rather than through an amended complaint under Rule 15(a). The post discusses how these rulings illustrate the importance of consistent legal theory development throughout litigation and the risks of shifting positions on appeal, particularly in class actions where the stakes extend beyond the named plaintiff.

blogs.title: Voluntary Cessation and the Burden of Proving Non-Recurrence in Wage-and-Hour Cases
blogs.description: This post focuses on the Eighth Circuit's remand instruction for the district court to determine whether Consilio's allegedly violative overtime policy remains in place, implicating the voluntary cessation doctrine. The post analyzes the standard from Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw that a claim becomes moot only when it is 'absolutely clear' the wrongful conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur, and examines how this standard applies in the employment context where employers can easily reinstate policies. The post considers the practical difficulties plaintiffs face in proving non-recurrence after partial compensation and the strategic implications for employers who pay wages but maintain disputed policies while seeking to moot penalty claims.
